title: Defend the Choke Point, Not the Product
documentTitle: United States v. Google LLC (Ad Tech) — PTX0367: Email from Jonathan Bellack to Paul Muret (September 6, 2016)
excerptForBlog: Personally, I really don't want to productize HB. I think it goes in the direct opposite direction of all our user experience efforts, and we need to double down on Jedi++ to make sure there's no business model that works in HB but not in our server-side solution. I also want to see us do the testing to establish how much HB hurts consumer metrics like latency, data usage, and battery; and advertiser metrics like viewability, CTR, brand lift, etc. We don't want anybody's HB to get an actual First Look ahead of everything else, because that puts GDN and DBM (and the AdX buyers) at risk. That is the concern about FAN or Amazon investing in HB — they could persuade publishers to say something like 'if we can pay you $10+, don't even bother checking with Google, just give it to us right away.' That makes HB the new yield manager. There will eventually be a limit on how many header calls a pub can send out without killing user experience. I still think the limit will be zero, but for sake of argument assume it's more like 3-5. That will push things toward server-to-server, but that could mean one HB company builds a more open Jedi than ours — more like Chris's 'Sith' product, where it's open season with no rules. Protecting reservations — yes, as long as we're the system of record for guarantees and guarantees are the most important part of publisher revenues, we will remain a must-call and HB has a limited ability to avoid calling DFP.

lessonTitle: Defend the Choke Point, Not the Product
pullQuote: When rivals attack your business model, your real moat is the one workflow they cannot route around.
leadershipTraits: uses data as a strategic weapon
situation: In September 2016, Google executive Jonathan Bellack emailed colleague Paul Muret about Header Bidding (HB) — a technique letting publishers auction ad inventory to multiple buyers simultaneously, outside Google's ad server. Bellack is working through whether Google should build its own version. The stakes: if HB catches on, buyers like Facebook's FAN or Amazon could offer publishers guaranteed high prices and cut Google out of the auction entirely.
insight: Bellack is not worried about Header Bidding as a feature. He's worried about it as a **bypass**. His line makes it plain: a rival could tell publishers 'if we can pay you $10+, don't even bother checking with Google.' That turns HB into 'the new yield manager' — and whoever controls yield management controls publisher relationships. This is a classic platform moat problem. Google's leverage rests on being the 'system of record for guarantees,' meaning publishers always have to call DFP (Google's ad server) to fulfill reserved deals. HB threatens that must-call status. Bellack's answer is twofold: make the server-side alternative (Jedi++) so good that HB offers no unique advantage, and use performance data — latency, battery, viewability — to slow publisher adoption. He also flags a second-order risk: if HB wins and goes server-to-server, a more open competitor ('Sith') could set the new rules for the whole ecosystem. He'd rather compete on his own terrain than let someone else define the playing field.
application: If a rival feature is gaining traction, map exactly which part of your business it bypasses — not just what it competes with. Then ask: what constraint (technical, contractual, economic) keeps customers still needing you? Reinforce that constraint while you close the feature gap. Don't just copy the rival; make their approach unnecessary.
